question: A 30-year-old man comes to the physician because of an episode of bloody vomiting this morning and a 1-week history of burning upper abdominal pain. Two weeks ago, he sustained a head injury and was in a coma for 3 days. An endoscopy shows multiple, shallow hemorrhagic lesions predominantly in the gastric fundus and greater curvature. Biopsies show patchy loss of epithelium and an acute inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria that does not extend beyond the muscularis mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Head injury -> Coma -> Stress ulcer -> Cushing ulcer -> 80% CHAIN: Burning upper abdominal pain -> Bloody vomiting -> Gastric mucosal injury -> Erosive gastritis -> 70% CHAIN: Endoscopy findings: multiple shallow hemorrhagic lesions in gastric fundus and greater curvature -> Biopsy findings: patchy loss of epithelium and acute inflammatory infiltrate in lamina propria -> Diagnosis: Erosive gastritis -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 30-year-old man with bloody vomiting and upper abdominal pain is erosive gastritis. The chain of events starting from the head injury leading to stress ulcer and then Cushing ulcer is not supported by consensus. The chain linking burning upper abdominal pain to bloody vomiting and gastric mucosal injury aligns with erosive gastritis. The endoscopy findings of multiple shallow hemorrhagic lesions in the gastric fundus and greater curvature, along with biopsy findings of patchy loss of epithelium and acute inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria, support the diagnosis of erosive gastritis.
analysis: The patient's presentation of bloody vomiting, upper abdominal pain, and endoscopic findings of multiple shallow hemorrhagic lesions with biopsy showing patchy loss of epithelium and acute inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria are consistent with erosive gastritis. The history of a head injury leading to stress ulcer and then Cushing ulcer is not well-supported by consensus. Erosive gastritis is the most likely diagnosis in this case.
